title: Breaking and Entering: Dick Diver
summary: Two of the members from Dick Diver – Steph Hughes and Al Montfort – delve into their feelings of anticipation regarding their upcoming shows at the Thornbury Theatre, sharing details of the line up and potential future gigs! They also discuss the experience of being reunited with the band and playing together again, 10 years after their last album release, while also reminising on their time in the music industry over the years.
transcript:
Steph Hughes and Al Montfort of Dick Diver joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studios, ahead of the band's reunion shows at the Thornbury Theatre, 10 years after their last album. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 22 May 2025. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: We're joined by two members of the band. Welcome to Al Montfort and Steph Hughes of Dick Diver. A band that needs no introduction, but for a little background: you formed back in 2008 and released those first EPs, then came the real breakthrough, your debut New Start Again, which we were talking about with Guy and Ben from Chapter Music. Such a landmark release. Then Calendar Days, and 2015's Melbourne, Florida, which was 10 years ago, which seems surreal. All of them made a huge impact, and they remain influential, beloved classics. So we're thrilled you've announced some shows. I hope you're feeling the love, because there's a collective excitement around it.

Steph: Yeah, it's been pretty wild. The way we operate, we really have to seize the moment when the bandmates are around. It's such a special event in itself just when all our bandmates are in the same place at the same time, and the fact that everyone else has got around it too was a great bonus. So we're like, might as well add a couple more shows. It's going to be four days at the Thornbury Theatre now.

Simon: I think we saw someone on socials calling for some kind of Las Vegas-style residency. We just want every night for a month.

Al: That's what I'm aiming for, yeah.

Lauren: Simon mentioned it's been 10 years since your most recent Dick Diver album, Melbourne, Florida, and you've said that now felt like the right time for these shows. What sparked the reunion?

Al: I think, like Steph said, just being all in the same city. It's great to just play together and see each other, but also I'd feel pretty guilty if we didn't play. I think the Melbourne community would be really angry.

Steph: It's a guilt and shame-based reunion, as always.

Lauren: Powerful motivators.

Al: The biggest motivator for us is definitely shame.

Simon: Well, joy is the overriding emotion, that's for sure, from the fans, the listeners and ourselves. The music speaks across generations, and it's still resonant. For yourselves, revisiting the catalogue in rehearsals, what feelings are emerging?

Al: We've had a couple of jams with just Steph, Al and myself, because we're all in Melbourne at the moment, and it's been kind of amazing, playing the songs again.

Steph: Instant, yeah. There's a bit of muscle memory in there. But afterwards, joy, joy. Less shame, more joy.

Al: When we were jamming, it felt pretty special.

Simon: Those songs evoke a particular period, maybe, for you as a band. Do they resonate in new and surprising ways now as well?

Steph: Yeah, they do to me. All bands are kind of like little teams, and they all have different dynamics. And with Dick Diver, it is seriously like riding a bike. We connect very easily with certain melodies and harmonies, the way we sync together, the way our instruments play together. We played together so much at one time, 15 years ago, that it really is a part of how we all play music now: what we take to other bands, and what we take playing in the world. So some of those things are more highlighted for me now that I've played music in different spaces.

And yet it is so joyous. I was like, 'Oh, this is amazing,' seeing Al again, because Al McKay, one of our guitarists, has moved back to Melbourne. He was in London for 10 years. So hopefully it's less of a rare thing for us all to be together now.

Lauren: Great to have him back. It's been a reflective show for us today. We spoke to Guy and Ben of Chapter Music earlier about their show at Rising, the end of an era for the label and the beginning of a new one. And of course you released your albums on Chapter. Can you tell us about your relationship with the label?

Al: I'm trying to think. Guy and Ben came to an early show. We supported Guy Blackman, I think.

Steph: Oh, yes. So they were there.

Al: Exactly. I think we were in the right spot: we played with Guy, and Sly Hats as well.

Steph: Oh, true. Geoffrey O'Connor's other band, other than Crayon Fields. What an era.

I think the relationship over time has been pretty involved, for a label. They like to discuss the finer points of releases; I heard Ben talking about sequences in the interview earlier. We've got our own ideas, and it's always good to get their input.

Al: But we're probably annoying for them as well.

Lauren: What has Chapter meant to you in terms of the broader musical community of the city?

Al: I was thinking about that before, when you asked what spurred these shows. Being a part of this community, a part of RRR, PBS, 3CR, the Melbourne music community, the people we've met through Chapter, everybody on Chapter: I think it's really important. When I say I would feel guilt and shame if we didn't play, maybe that's back to shame.

Lauren: It's a bit of a pattern.

Al: I think it's as much for all our friends and all our fellow community members as well as for ourselves. When we ended up releasing music on Chapter, we were sort of instantly a part, instantly embedded in a lot of amazing communities that Guy and Ben had kind of paved before. So that's initially why we all connected, and I'm super grateful for that kind of community work they've done.

Steph: And it is a community. We feel so lucky.

Simon: What Chapter are doing and what you're doing are so aligned, interconnected parts of that larger extended family. It's really beautiful to see. And these shows are going to be a family affair: 18-plus, but all-ages as well. That must have been important, with a whole new generation discovering you through their family's CD collections and records.

Al: I hope so. It's actually a bit of a childcare co-op scenario we've got going on, because there are multiple kids involved, and I've got one in the studio right now who's doing a great job on quality control. A lot of our friends have kids, and we just wanted it to be a big gathering for everyone who can come.

Lauren: Everyone's so excited to see you play again. There's that famous story of people jumping the fence during your set at Laneway one year. Should we expect something similar this time?

Al: They weren't jumping the fence to see us. Vance Joy was playing on the stage next to us, I think.

Steph: Vance Joy's a renowned sweetie, though. At the airport lounge I was like, 'This guy is a legend.'

Al: Absolute legend. So we were like, 'Fair enough. Run past us.'

Lauren: Can we ask about the line-up? We've just announced another show at the Thornbury Theatre today, an all-ages show on Sunday 3 August. Who have you invited to play with you?

Steph: Kankawa Nagarra. Well, where do I start? We're such fans. Her record Wirlmarni won the Australian Music Prize last year, and it's been non-stop for me. I love it so much. She just writes really timeless and intuitive tracks.

She's coming all the way from the Kimberley, from about 100K outside Fitzroy Crossing. It's an extremely long way to get to us, but Al's — you've done a lot of amazing booking work — so we've got her coming down. She's accompanied by our friend Darren Hanlon, who's done a lot of touring with her in the outback, and they're about to go to Europe together. She's 80 years old, and apparently she's just really keen to do all these adventures. I was like, maybe she might be tired, or want to do some other stuff closer to home, and he's like, 'Nah, she's frothing.' So she's ready to go. She's also played a couple of times with Darren's kids, so I know she's great for older folks and younger folks. She's just an incredible performer. So stoked.

Simon: No shame or expectation with this next question, but now that it's a bit easier to get together, is there anything on the horizon, other gigs or future releases?

Al: There's a record that's nearly finished. This is a shame thing on me, because I'm definitely one of the handbrakes.

Simon: It's a shame-free space. But that's incredible news. So that's something you've been working on?

Al: Yeah. It's been a fair while. The last time we were able to hang out in real life, we put the bones of it together, and since then it's just been overdubbing. But a couple of kids and life and all that stuff. I feel super motivated to get it out one day.

Steph: Watch this space. We've got lots there, and any time we're together, we'd like to play gigs. It's just natural that we feel like it. We're all really good friends, you know.

Lauren: Well, we're all absolutely rapt that Dick Diver are back playing shows, with a new album on the way.
